title: Nectar mixed with poison
hookLine: Sita asks how Rama really is, and Hanuman's honest answer is sweet and bitter at once
carry: viraha: the ache of missing is love too

lines: DOES HE STILL THINK OF ME?
cards: Sita has the ring in her hand, and now she asks the questions anyone asks about someone far away. Not the news. The person.
Is Rama well? Does he still think of me? Has his love grown cold with distance?
When a friend comes back from seeing someone you love, those are the questions that come first.

teach.b: Hanuman answers honestly, and his answer is a portrait of a man in grief. Rama can barely sleep. When he wakes, the first word out of him is Sita.
He doesn't notice the insects that land on him. When he sees a lovely flower, he sighs and says her name. He is wasting away with sorrow, Hanuman says, but he is preparing, and he is coming.
Now listen to how Sita receives it.

What you've told me, she says, is nectar mixed with poison. Nectar, because Rama hasn't forgotten her; every detail of his grief proves his love. Poison, because the man she loves is suffering, and she can't reach him.
Hindu devotion has a name for this ache: viraha, love in separation. And it doesn't treat the ache as a problem to fix. It honors it as one of the deepest forms of love there is.
The gopis of Vrindavan, longing for Krishna after he leaves, are its great example, and Mirabai's songs are full of it.

teach.h: YOU CAN ONLY MISS WHAT YOU LOVE.
teach.b: Many teachers say longing for God is already a kind of meeting, because you can only miss what you love. Rama and Sita, an ocean apart, each saying the other's name, are viraha in its plainest form.
That's why a bhajan can be sad and happy at once, and why people cry while singing one and call it sweet.

how: Devotional readings of the Sundara Kanda dwell on Rama's grief and on Sita's phrase 'nectar mixed with poison', and many bhajans sing of viraha, the longing of separation, as love itself.

o: a gift Hanuman buys for Sita in Lanka's market
the jewel Ravana took from Sita when he carried her off
the token that opens Sita's questions about how Rama really is

games.q: how is he? — tap the pairs.

s: Hanuman tells Sita that Rama is fine, to spare her
Sita calls Hanuman's words nectar mixed with poison
sweet because Rama loves her, bitter because he suffers.
in Hindu devotion, longing for God means you've failed
viraha, love in separation, is honored as one of love's deepest forms.

games.q: a friend hears a bhajan about missing Krishna and says a song that sad can't be a happy one. by today's story, what fits?
o: it can be both: viraha, the ache of missing, is a form of love.
they're right: sad bhajans are only for funerals.
the singer must be angry at Krishna.
games.why: Sita called news of Rama's grief nectar mixed with poison. Hindu devotion calls that ache viraha, and treasures it.

practice: Bring to mind someone you miss, near or far, or gone. If you pray, offer the missing itself, the way bhajans do, with two names on the breath: Sita as you breathe in, Ram as you breathe out.
If you don't pray, simply let the ache be there, and notice the love inside it: sweet and bitter in one cup, neither canceling the other.

wordCard.voice: The ring. The token that opens Sita's questions about Rama, and Hanuman's honest answer, which Sita calls nectar mixed with poison.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi viraha, separation: the ache of love apart, sung in many bhajans.

carryVoice: Your line: viraha, the ache of missing is love too. Tomorrow, Sita's doubts, spoken out loud. That's day six hundred twenty-one.
